# Founding and Early History

Istanbul's documented history begins around 660 BC when Greek settlers from Megara established Byzantium on the European side of the Bosphorus. Archaeological evidence suggests even earlier settlement, with Neolithic artifacts indicating habitation as far back as the sixth millennium BC. The city was named Byzantium by its Megarian founders.

# Historical Names

The city has carried three primary names reflecting its successive periods of dominance. Byzantium served as the original Greek designation. Constantinople emerged following Constantine the Great's refoundation in 330 AD, deriving from the Latin name Constantinus, after Constantine the Great, the Roman emperor who refounded the city in 324 AD. The modern name Istanbul derives from the Medieval Greek phrase eis ten Polin, literally 'to the city', and was officially adopted in 1930.

# Byzantine Era

Constantinople was proclaimed capital of the Roman Empire on May 11, 330. Following the empire's division in 395, the city became the capital of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire, serving in this role until 1453. During this period numerous churches were built across the city, including Hagia Sophia, built during the reign of Justinian I, which remained the world's largest cathedral for a thousand years.

# Ottoman Period

The Ottomans conquered Constantinople on May 29, 1453. Sultan Mehmed II declared it the new Ottoman capital and undertook massive urban revitalization. The city remained the capital of the Ottoman Empire and seat of its caliphate for nearly five centuries, until the empire's dissolution following World War I.

# Turkish Republic

Following Turkish independence (1919-1922), the new Turkish Republic established its capital in Ankara in 1923. The city's official name changed to Istanbul on March 28, 1930. From the 1930s onward, with large-scale urban planning efforts initially led by Henri Prost between 1936 and 1950, Istanbul underwent significant structural modernization.

# Geographic Position

Istanbul occupies a strategic location straddling the Bosphorus strait. The city is uniquely positioned on two continents; about two-thirds of its population live in Europe and the rest in Asia. It sits between the Sea of Marmara and the Black Sea in northwestern Turkey. This geographic positioning along major historical trade routes, particularly the historic Silk Road and maritime passages, fundamentally shaped its development and significance.
